title: How agents broke app-level infrastructure - Evan Boyle

primary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is durable execution, long-running workflows, retries, resumability, and crash-safe agent orchestration via Redis streams and worker-draining deployment patterns, directly matching orchestration_durable_execution.

summary: Evan Boyle traces the AI engineer's journey from simple prompt-and-tool-call prototypes to complex, long-running workflows that increasingly resemble data engineering pipelines. As workflows grow from seconds to minutes, engineers must crawl inboxes, ingest GitHub repos, and process many artifacts, each requiring numerous LLM calls. This exposes a fundamental mismatch between modern AI workloads and the infrastructure designed for Web 2.0, where p99 latency was a few hundred milliseconds and anything slower triggered pager alerts. Today, LLM APIs have p99 latency of multiple seconds, and even major providers like OpenAI and Gemini experience overlapping outages, while rate limits constrain bursty traffic from batch processing and onboarding. Existing solutions—Rube Goldberg machines on SQS, data engineering tools like Airflow, and durable execution engines like Temporal—were designed for niches and often by Java engineers, which doesn't appeal to TypeScript-focused full-stack developers. Mainstream serverless providers compound the problem: most timeout after five minutes, some limit outbound HTTP requests, and none offer native streaming or resumability. Boyle illustrates two product experiences demanding better infrastructure: background onboarding where users ingest data via hundreds of LLM calls while immediately using the product, and content generation agents running 3-4 minutes that must survive page refreshes and intermediate errors without losing context. To address this, Boyle's team built an open-source anti-framework inspired by React's component model, providing reusable, idempotent, independently testable components and workflows composed from those components. Each component gets retry boundaries, error boundaries, and tracing. Workflows automatically generate REST APIs supporting synchronous and asynchronous invocation, plus streams for intermediate status and final output. The framework deploys to a purpose-built serverless platform with separated API and compute layers communicating exclusively through Redis streams, enabling independent scaling, resumability, heartbeat-based monitoring, automatic restart on crash, and bring-your-own compute support. Boyle closes with practical lessons: start simple since nobody writes hour-long workflows on day one, but plan for a long-running future as coding agents and deep research experiences become common. Keep compute and API planes separate, lean on Redis streams for resumability, let users navigate away without losing progress, and handle errors transparently. He warns that deploying long-running workflows requires careful worker draining and blue-green deployment patterns—the devil is in the details, easy to get started but hard to get right. The implementation is available as GenSx on GitHub.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the AI engineer journey
sections.summary: Evan Boyle introduces himself as founder/CEO of Genisx and early Pulumi employee. He traces the AI engineer journey from simple prompts and tool calls to complex workflows chaining tailored prompts, then to data engineering as context ingestion becomes the hardest problem.

sections.title: Infrastructure assumptions have changed
sections.summary: Boyle contrasts Web 2.0 millisecond latency with LLM applications' multi-second p99 latency. He shows outage patterns from OpenAI and Gemini that overlap, undermining failover strategies, and describes rate limits constraining bursty traffic patterns.

sections.title: Current solutions and their limitations
sections.summary: Existing tools for long-running workflows (SQS, Airflow, Temporal) don't suit TypeScript full-stack developers. Serverless providers timeout after ~5 minutes, limit outbound HTTP, lack native streaming, and don't support resumability needed when users refresh pages during multi-minute workflows.

sections.title: Product experiences requiring long-running workflows
sections.summary: Two examples: onboarding where background ingestion via hundreds of LLM calls runs while users immediately use the product, and a content generation agent running 3-4 minutes that must survive page refreshes and intermediate errors. Speaker describes friction experimenting with longer workflows due to serverless constraints.

sections.title: The anti-framework: composable components and workflows
sections.summary: Boyle introduces an open-source anti-framework inspired by React's component model. Components are reusable, idempotent, independently testable steps using a wrapped OpenAI SDK. Workflows compose components with retry boundaries, error boundaries, tracing, and auto-generated REST APIs supporting sync/async invocation and streaming.

sections.title: Architecture: separated API and compute layers with Redis streams
sections.summary: The framework deploys to a serverless platform with separated API and compute layers communicating via Redis streams. This enables independent scaling, resumability across page refreshes, heartbeat-based monitoring with automatic restart, and bring-your-own compute since the compute layer is stateless.

sections.title: Resumability, lessons, and deployment considerations
sections.summary: Boyle emphasizes resuming directly from Redis streams so page refreshes don't lose progress. He advises starting simple but planning for long-running futures as coding agents and deep research become common. Key lessons include keeping compute and API planes separate, using Redis streams for resumability, allowing users to navigate away without losing progress, and handling errors transparently. He warns that deploying workflows running 60 minutes requires careful worker draining and blue-green deployment patterns—easy to start but hard to get right. He directs the audience to GenSx on GitHub.
